blocks.x: Chapter 1 ended on a promise. 1.4 called two expressions equivalent when they agree at every value, and said the rules for rewriting one form into another would arrive in Chapter 2. This lesson delivers the first one, and it begins as a way to multiply ugly numbers in your head.
Compute \(9\cdot 204\) in your head. The number \(204\) splits into \(200+4\), and each piece is easy to multiply by \(9\). Multiply both pieces, then add. What do you get?
hints: Multiply the easy pieces, \(9\cdot 200\) and \(9\cdot 4\), then add the two results.
blocks.sol: \(9\cdot 200=1800\) and \(9\cdot 4=36\), so the total is \(1800+36=\boxed{1836}\). Splitting a number into easy pieces beats grinding through it digit by digit.

blocks.x: The distributive property. For any numbers, \(a(b+c)=ab+ac\). The reason is one count taken two ways. Take \(a\) groups, each holding \(b+c\) items. Counting whole groups gives \(a(b+c)\) items, while counting the \(b\)s and the \(c\)s separately gives \(ab+ac\), and the totals must match because they count the same items. That is what the last problem did with \(9(200+4)\). The rules in 1.3 each concerned a single operation, and this is the first law connecting addition and multiplication to each other. As an instruction it reads, the outside factor multiplies each inside piece.
Compute \(6\cdot 398\) the same way, but treat \(398\) as \(400-2\). Multiply each piece by \(6\), then correct for the extra. What is the product?
hints: Round \(398\) up to \(400\), multiply, then pay back the \(6\cdot 2\) you borrowed.
blocks.sol: \(6\cdot 400=2400\) and \(6\cdot 2=12\), so the product is \(2400-12=\boxed{2388}\). The correction comes off rather than on, since \(398\) sits \(2\) below \(400\).

blocks.x: Distribution over subtraction. The companion form \(a(b-c)=ab-ac\) is not a second law. By 1.3, subtracting \(c\) is adding \(-c\), so \(a(b-c)=a(b+(-c))=ab+a(-c)=ab-ac\), the same property applied to a sum. One sentence now covers both forms. The outside factor multiplies each inside piece, and each piece keeps the sign it came with. In \(6(400-2)\) the second piece is \(-2\), which is why the \(12\) was subtracted rather than added.

blocks.cap: Both bands show one fact. On top, a sheet's area is counted whole as \(7(x+4)\) or piece by piece as \(7x+28\), and the two counts measure the same sheet. Below, four rows of dots are counted row by row as \(4(10+2)\) or by color as \(40+8\), landing on \(48\) either way. One thing counted two ways must give one total, and that is the whole proof of \(a(b+c)=ab+ac\).

Nothing in the rule requires the inside pieces to be plain numbers. Expand \(7(n+6)\). The result has two terms, one with \(n\) and one without. Enter the constant term of the result, the term with no \(n\).
hints: The \(7\) multiplies both pieces inside, the \(n\) and the \(6\), not just the first.
blocks.sol: Distributing to both pieces gives \(7\cdot n+7\cdot 6=7n+42\), so the term with no \(n\) is \(\boxed{42}\). Writing \(7n+6\), with the \(7\) multiplying only the first piece, is the classic mistake.

blocks.x: Expanding. Rewriting \(7(n+6)\) as \(7n+42\) is called expanding, and the outside factor multiplies every term inside. The result is not merely similar, it is equivalent, equal at every value of \(n\). That settles a debt from 1.4, where \(6(t+2)\) and \(6t+12\) matched at one input, a good sign but not proof. One application of the distributive property now proves it, \(6(t+2)=6t+12\) at every \(t\). Checking values can disprove, distribution can prove. One reading note, an expanded result has a coefficient and a constant term, so enter the part the question names.
Expand \(5(3w-4)\). The first inside piece already carries a coefficient, and the second carries a minus sign. Enter the coefficient of \(w\) in the result.
hints: The minus belongs to the \(4\). Multiply \(5\) by \(3w\), then \(5\) by \(-4\), keeping that sign.
blocks.sol: \(5\cdot 3w=15w\) and \(5\cdot(-4)=-20\), so the result is \(15w-20\) and the coefficient of \(w\) is \(\boxed{15}\). The minus stays attached to the \(4\), which is what keeps the constant at \(-20\).

blocks.x: Expand \(g(g+11)\). The outside factor is now the variable itself, and 1.5 already settled what \(g\cdot g\) is. Enter the coefficient of the plain-\(g\) term of the result, not the \(g^2\) term.
hints: By 1.5, \(g\cdot g=g^2\). The other product is \(g\cdot 11\).
blocks.sol: Distributing gives \(g\cdot g+g\cdot 11=g^2+11g\). The plain-\(g\) term is \(11g\), so its coefficient is \(\boxed{11}\). The \(g^2\) term has a coefficient too, namely \(1\), but it belongs to the other term.

blocks.x: The outside factor can be a variable. The rule holds for any numbers, and a variable stands for a number, so the factor outside the parentheses can be a letter, \(g(g+11)=g\cdot g+g\cdot 11=g^2+11g\). Each product follows rules already in hand, \(g\cdot g=g^2\) by 1.5's count of factors, and \(g\cdot 11\) is written \(11g\) with the coefficient first. Every term inside still gets multiplied. Nothing in the rule depends on what the outside factor is, a number, a letter, or a larger expression built from both.
A student expands \(8(y+3)\) and writes \(8y+3\), multiplying only the first term inside. Evaluate both expressions at \(y=2\), each on its own. How far apart are their values?
hints: Substitute \(y=2\) into \(8(y+3)\) and into \(8y+3\) separately, then compare the two numbers.
blocks.sol: At \(y=2\), the original is \(8(2+3)=8\cdot 5=40\), while the student's version is \(8\cdot 2+3=19\), so the gap is \(40-19=\boxed{21}\). By 1.4, one input where two expressions disagree is enough to show they are not equivalent.

blocks.x: Partial distribution. The most common expanding error is multiplying only the first term, claiming \(a(b+c)=ab+c\). That claim is false, and one evaluation at any convenient value exposes it, the same checking move 1.6 practiced. One input, two different outputs, and the claim fails. The fix is mechanical. A factor sitting against parentheses multiplies every term inside, every time, however many terms there are.

A bare minus sign directly in front of parentheses means multiplication by \(-1\), so \(-(4d-7)\) means \((-1)(4d-7)\). Rewrite it by distributing that \(-1\) over both inside terms. Enter the constant term of the result.
hints: Both inside terms get multiplied by \(-1\), so both signs flip, not just the first.
blocks.sol: Distributing hits both terms, \((-1)(4d)=-4d\) and \((-1)(-7)=+7\), so the result is \(-4d+7\) and the constant term is \(\boxed{7}\). Flipping only the first sign, giving \(-4d-7\), is the standard error.

blocks.x: Distributing \(-1\). A bare minus in front of parentheses is multiplication by \(-1\), so every sign inside flips, positive terms turning negative and negative terms turning positive. Nothing new is involved, this is the distributive property with \(a=-1\), and since the product of two negatives is positive, the \(-7\) inside came out as \(+7\). Make the full flip a habit now. You will use it constantly when 2.3 subtracts whole expressions, and flipping only the first sign is among the most common sign errors in all of algebra.
The rule works for any number of inside terms. Compute \(12\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{4}\right)\) by distributing the \(12\) over all three terms. What value comes out?
hints: Each product, \(12\cdot\frac{1}{2}\), \(12\cdot\frac{1}{3}\), and \(12\cdot\frac{1}{4}\), is a whole number.
blocks.sol: \(12\cdot\frac{1}{2}+12\cdot\frac{1}{3}+12\cdot\frac{1}{4}=6+4+3=\boxed{13}\). Adding the fractions first gives \(\frac{13}{12}\) and lands in the same place, but distributing skips the common denominator entirely.

blocks.x: A number trick. Think of a number, add \(5\), triple the result, subtract \(15\), then divide by \(3\). Start with \(47\) and follow the four steps in order. What number comes out?
hints: Follow the four steps one at a time, keeping each intermediate result.
When you finish, compare the number that came out with the number that went in.
blocks.sol: The steps take \(47\) to \(52\) to \(156\) to \(141\) and back to \(\boxed{47}\). Writing the start as \(n\), the first three steps build \(3(n+5)-15=3n+15-15=3n\), and dividing by \(3\) leaves \(n\), so whatever goes in comes back out.

blocks.x: When two parenthesized expressions multiply each other, as in \((x+2)(x+3)\), the distributive property simply runs twice, once for each term of the first factor. That door opens with quadratics in Chapter 9.

The first rewriting tool is in hand. Ugly products split into easy pieces, and parentheses open without changing an expression's value at any input, which is exactly what 1.4 meant by equivalent. Next, 2.2 puts evaluation to work on heavier expressions, and in 2.3 this rule runs in reverse, reading \(ab+ac\) as \(a(b+c)\), a move called factoring.

review.x: Mental math first. Compute \(8\cdot 306\) in your head by splitting \(306\) into \(300+6\) and multiplying each piece by \(8\). Enter the product.
hints: \(8\cdot 300\) and \(8\cdot 6\) are both easy. Add the two results.
review.sol: A common slip is to lose the middle zero and compute \(8\cdot 36=288\), which is way too small for eight copies of a number near \(300\). Keep the pieces as \(300\) and \(6\). Then \(8\cdot 300=2400\) and \(8\cdot 6=48\), so \(8\cdot 306=2400+48=\boxed{2448}\).

review.x: Compute \(4\cdot 997\) by treating \(997\) as \(1000-3\). Multiply each piece by \(4\), then correct for the overshoot. Enter the product.
hints: The product \(4\cdot 1000\) overshoots, and \(4\cdot 3\) measures by how much.
review.sol: Over subtraction the rule reads \(4(1000-3)=4\cdot 1000-4\cdot 3\). Adding the correction instead of subtracting it gives \(4012\), the wrong direction, since \(997\) sits below \(1000\). The product is \(4000-12=\boxed{3988}\).

review.x: Expand \(9(u+7)\) by multiplying each inside term by \(9\). Enter the constant term of the result, the term with no \(u\).
hints: The \(9\) multiplies both pieces inside the parentheses, not just the \(u\).
review.sol: Multiplying only the first term gives \(9u+7\), the partial-distribution error, and \(9u+7\) is not equivalent to \(9(u+7)\). The \(9\) multiplies the \(7\) as well, so the expansion is \(9u+63\) and the constant term is \(\boxed{63}\).

review.x: Expand \(6(5h-9)\), keeping each inside term's sign as you distribute. Enter the coefficient of \(h\) in the result, the number multiplying it.
hints: The minus belongs to the \(9\), so the second product comes out negative.
review.sol: Both products keep their signs, \(6\cdot 5h=30h\) and \(6\cdot(-9)=-54\), so the expansion is \(30h-54\). Entering \(-54\) answers the wrong part, and writing \(+54\) loses the sign. The coefficient of \(h\) is \(\boxed{30}\).

review.x: Expand \(t(t+17)\). The outside factor is a variable this time. Enter the coefficient of the plain-\(t\) term of the result, not the \(t^2\) term.
hints: The outside factor multiplies both terms inside. One product is \(t\) times \(t\), and the other product is the one that makes the plain-\(t\) term.
review.sol: The outside factor multiplies both terms, \(t\cdot t=t^2\) and \(t\cdot 17=17t\), so the expansion is \(t^2+17t\). It is tempting to answer with the coefficient of \(t^2\), which is \(1\), or to type the whole term \(17t\), but the question asks only for the coefficient of the plain-\(t\) term. That term is \(17t\), so the answer is \(\boxed{17}\).

review.x: Rewrite \(-(6p-19)\) by distributing the minus. A bare minus in front of parentheses means multiplication by \(-1\). Enter the constant term of the result.
hints: The bare minus means multiply by \(-1\), so both inside signs flip.
review.sol: Flipping only the first sign gives \(-6p-19\), the usual error. Multiplying each term by \(-1\) gives \(-6p\) and \((-1)(-19)=+19\), so the result is \(-6p+19\) and the constant term is \(\boxed{19}\).

review.x: A student claims that \(5(x+8)=5x+8\). Settle it the 1.4 way, evaluate both expressions at \(x=3\). How far apart are their values?
hints: Substitute \(3\) into each expression separately, the grouped one inside first.
review.sol: At \(x=3\), \(5(x+8)=5\cdot 11=55\) while \(5x+8=15+8=23\). Entering \(55\) or \(23\) alone answers a different question, the ask is the gap between them. One disagreement proves the claim false, and the gap is \(55-23=\boxed{32}\).

review.x: Three terms and two letters this time. Expand \(5(2a+9b-7)\), multiplying every term by \(5\). Enter the coefficient of \(a\).
hints: Three terms inside means three products, and only one of them involves \(a\).
review.sol: The \(5\) multiplies all three terms, giving \(10a+45b-35\). The ask names the coefficient of \(a\), so \(45\) and \(-35\) answer the wrong part. It is \(5\cdot 2=\boxed{10}\).

review.x: Compute \(15\left(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{5}\right)\) by distributing the \(15\) over both fractions. Done this way, no common denominator is needed.
hints: \(15\) times each fraction comes out whole.
review.sol: Adding the fractions first gives \(\frac{16}{15}\) and also works, but distributing skips the common denominator entirely. \(15\cdot\frac{2}{3}=10\) and \(15\cdot\frac{2}{5}=6\), so the value is \(10+6=\boxed{16}\).

review.x: Compute \(7\cdot 8.03\) by splitting \(8.03\) into \(8+0.03\). Decimals distribute the same way whole numbers do. Enter the exact product.
hints: Two products, \(7\cdot 8\) and \(7\cdot 0.03\), then add them.
review.sol: The split gives \(7\cdot 8=56\) and \(7\cdot 0.03=0.21\). Misplacing the decimal point to get \(2.1\) ruins the sum, so keep \(0.21\) and the product is \(56+0.21=\boxed{56.21}\).

review.x: Expand \(3(z^2+6z+9)\). The inside has three terms, one of them squared, so the result has three terms too. Enter the constant term.
hints: The \(3\) multiplies all three terms, the squared one included.
review.sol: Every term gets the factor, so the expansion is \(3z^2+18z+27\). Stopping after two terms and leaving the \(9\) untouched is the partial-distribution error again. The constant term is \(\boxed{27}\).

review.x: Whatever number \(k\) stands for, the expression \(4(k+6)-4k\) comes out to the same value every time. Enter that value.
hints: Distribute the \(4\) over \(k+6\) first.
After distributing, look at the two \(k\) terms side by side.
review.sol: The tempting slip is to distribute the \(4\) onto \(k\) only and write \(4k+6-4k\), which would leave \(6\). The \(4\) multiplies both terms inside the parentheses, so distributing gives \(4k+24-4k\). The \(4k\) and \(-4k\) cancel completely, leaving \(24\) no matter what \(k\) is. That is the same cancellation that forced the number trick's output earlier in the lesson. The value is \(\boxed{24}\).

blocks.x: Evaluating was settled in 1.6, so nothing about the method changes here, the expressions just get heavier. Substitute in parentheses, compute by the order of operations, read off one number. This lesson is six problems, and each one adds a step the last did not have.

Evaluate \(5-4y\) at \(y=-7\). There are two minus signs in the second term, one printed in the expression and one that comes with the value, so write the substitution with parentheses to keep them separate.
hints: Read \(4(-7)\) as one finished product before subtracting anything.
blocks.sol: Substituting in parentheses gives \(5-4(-7)\). The product is \(4(-7)=-28\), and subtracting \(-28\) is adding \(28\), so the value is \(5+28=\boxed{33}\). Losing the value's sign turns the line into \(5-28=-23\), which is exactly what the parentheses prevent.

blocks.x: Evaluate \(\dfrac{3k}{4}+\dfrac{20}{k}\) at \(k=8\). The variable sits under a fraction bar this time, and it appears in two places at once. Enter the value as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Both \(k\)s become \(8\) at the same moment, one above a bar and one below, and each bar finishes as its own division.
blocks.sol: Substituting gives \(\frac{3(8)}{4}+\frac{20}{8}\). Each bar finishes as its own division, \(\frac{24}{4}=6\) and \(\frac{20}{8}=\frac{5}{2}\), so the value is \(6+\frac{5}{2}=\boxed{\dfrac{17}{2}}\). Combining across the bars into \(\frac{24+20}{4+8}\) merges two separate divisions into one and is wrong.

blocks.x: Same habits, heavier loads. Every problem here runs on the routine from 1.6, substitute in parentheses at every appearance, then work by the order from 1.2, writing each intermediate value down. What changes is where the variable sits. A letter can stand anywhere a number can, including under a fraction bar, and the bar still groups its whole top and its whole bottom. Writing the middle values down costs a few seconds and catches most sign errors before they compound.
Evaluate \(\sqrt{-12w}\) at \(w=-3\). The minus printed under the bar looks like the even-root trouble from 1.5. Substitute first, then decide whether the root exists.
hints: Compute the number actually under the bar once \(w\) is replaced, then judge.
blocks.sol: Substituting puts \(-12(-3)=36\) under the bar, and \(\sqrt{36}=\boxed{6}\). The minus printed in \(-12w\) is not the sign of the value, so rejecting the root on sight would throw away a perfectly good number.

blocks.x: Judge after substituting. An even root needs a nonnegative value under its bar, the rule from 1.5, and the sign that matters is the sign of the value after substituting, never the sign printed in the expression. \(-12w\) opens with a minus on the page, yet it is positive whenever \(w\) is negative. That is the same point as in 1.1, what a symbol looks like does not tell you its value. Compute what sits under the bar first, and only then decide whether the root exists.

blocks.cap: On top, the grey route rejects \(\sqrt{-4q}\) at sight from the printed minus, which judges the expression instead of the value. Substituting \(q=-25\) puts \(-4(-25)=100\) under the bar, so the root exists and equals \(10\). Below, \((2u+3)^2\) at \(u=9\) runs inside out, the innermost \(u\) becomes \(9\), the parentheses finish as \(21\), and squaring last gives \(441\).

blocks.x: Evaluate \(n^2-5n+3\) at \(n=-2\). Three terms, three sign decisions, one value, and every appearance of \(n\) gets its own parentheses.
hints: Write the parentheses at both appearances of \(n\) before doing any arithmetic.
Subtracting \(5(-2)\) is subtracting a negative.
blocks.sol: Substituting at both appearances gives \((-2)^2-5(-2)+3\). That is \(4+10+3=\boxed{17}\). Two slips are common here, reading the square as \(-2^2=-4\), and dropping the sign in the middle term when \(-5(-2)\) is really \(+10\).

blocks.x: Evaluate \((2h-3)^2+h\) at \(h=6\). The parentheses hold a whole expression this time. Build the inside value first, square the result, then finish the sum.
hints: The exponent applies to the whole parenthesized value, so finish \(2h-3\) before squaring anything.
blocks.sol: Inside first, \(2(6)-3=9\). Squaring gives \(9^2=81\), and the total is \(81+6=\boxed{87}\). The exponent takes the finished inside value, so squaring term by term into \(144-9+6=141\) is wrong.

blocks.x: Inside out with variables. A compound expression evaluates as a chain of small evaluations, innermost pieces first, which is the inside-out rule from 1.2 applied to substituted values. In \((2h-3)^2+h\), the inside finished as \(9\), the \(9\) fed the square, and the \(81\) fed the final sum. Each intermediate number is the input to the next layer, so a long expression is never one giant computation, it is many short ones in a row.

This one uses every skill from the lesson. Evaluate \(\dfrac{\sqrt{1-12v}}{v}\) at \(v=-4\). The bar covers all of \(1-12v\), the input is negative, and a division finishes the job. Enter the value as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Substitute before touching the root, so compute \(1-12(-4)\) under the bar first.
After taking the root, divide by \(v\) itself. Its value is \(-4\), sign included.
blocks.sol: Under the bar, \(1-12(-4)=1+48=49\), so the top is \(\sqrt{49}=7\). The bottom is \(v=-4\), and \(7\div(-4)=\boxed{-\dfrac{7}{4}}\). Two slips lurk here, stopping at the radical because of the printed minus, and dropping the denominator's sign to land on \(\dfrac{7}{4}\).

blocks.label: Fun fact
blocks.x: A GPS receiver finds your distance from each satellite by evaluating a compound expression, squared differences feeding a square root, inside out, many times every second.

The expressions got heavier and the method never changed. Parentheses on every substitution, signs judged after substituting, computation run from the inside out. Next, 2.3 turns the distributive property around, reading \(ab+ac\) as \(a(b+c)\), a rewrite called factoring.

review.x: Evaluate \(9-2t\) at \(t=-3\).
hints: Substitute with parentheses, then finish the product \(2(-3)\) before subtracting it.
review.sol: Substituting gives \(9-2(-3)\). The product is \(-6\), and subtracting \(-6\) is adding \(6\), so the value is \(9+6=\boxed{15}\). Without the parentheses the term reads \(2\cdot 3\) and the answer comes out \(3\).

review.x: Evaluate \(\dfrac{m}{3}+m\) at \(m=12\).
hints: Only the first \(m\) sits under the bar. The second one is a plain \(12\) added on.
review.sol: Only the first term sits over the bar, so it is \(12\div 3=4\), and the value is \(4+12=\boxed{16}\). The bar groups only its own top, so pulling the lone \(m\) underneath into \(\frac{12+12}{3}\) is wrong.

review.x: Evaluate \(\sqrt{2-7d}\) at \(d=-2\). Substitute before judging the root.
hints: Find the number actually under the bar once \(d\) is replaced.
review.sol: Substituting gives \(-7(-2)=14\), so the bar holds \(2+14=16\) and \(\sqrt{16}=\boxed{4}\). What decides whether an even root exists is the sign of the value after substituting, not the sign printed in the expression.

review.x: Evaluate \(w^2+3w\) at \(w=-18\).
hints: The square takes the whole value, sign included.
review.sol: Substituting gives \((-18)^2+3(-18)\), which is \(324-54=\boxed{270}\). The square takes the whole value with its sign, so \((-18)^2=324\). Reading it as \(-18^2=-324\) drops the total to \(-378\).

review.x: Evaluate \((3g-4)^2\) at \(g=5\).
hints: Finish the whole inside \(3g-4\) before squaring anything.
review.sol: Inside first, \(3(5)-4=11\), and \(11^2=\boxed{121}\). The exponent applies to the finished parenthesized value, so squaring \(g\) alone into \(3(25)-4=71\) is wrong.

review.x: Evaluate \(\dfrac{40}{p}-p\) at \(p=-5\).
hints: The divisor keeps its sign, and so does the subtracted \(p\).
review.sol: The first term is \(40\div(-5)=-8\), and subtracting \(p\) means subtracting \(-5\), so the value is \(-8+5=\boxed{-3}\). The divisor and the subtracted \(p\) both keep their signs, and dropping either one lands you on \(13\).

review.x: Evaluate \(\sqrt{h^2+63}\) at \(h=-1\).
hints: \(h^2\) means \((-1)^2\). Judge its sign after substituting.
review.sol: \((-1)^2=1\), so the bar holds \(1+63=64\), and \(\sqrt{64}=\boxed{8}\). Reading the square as \(-1^2=-1\) leaves \(62\) under the bar, which has no clean root, a good sign you took the sign wrong.

review.x: Evaluate \(\dfrac{a^2+b}{a+b}\) at \(a=-3\) and \(b=6\).
hints: Finish the whole top and the whole bottom before dividing.
review.sol: The top is \((-3)^2+6=15\) and the bottom is \(-3+6=3\), so the value is \(15\div 3=\boxed{5}\). Finish the whole top and the whole bottom before dividing, and remember \(a^2\) means \((-3)^2=9\), not \(-9\).

review.x: Evaluate \(2c^2-c^3\) at \(c=-3\).
hints: An odd power of a negative keeps the sign, an even power clears it.
review.sol: The even power clears the sign, so \(2(-3)^2=18\), and the odd power keeps it, so \((-3)^3=-27\). Then \(18-(-27)=18+27=\boxed{45}\). Treating the cube as \(+27\) gives \(-9\) instead.

review.x: Evaluate \(\dfrac{\sqrt{50-t^2}}{t+12}\) at \(t=-5\). Enter the value as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: \(t^2\) means \((-5)^2\). Settle what sits under the bar first.
Finish the whole top, then the whole bottom, and divide last.
review.sol: The bar holds \(50-(-5)^2=50-25=25\), so the top is \(5\). The bottom is \(-5+12=7\), and the value is \(\boxed{\dfrac{5}{7}}\). Both halves turn on signs, \((-5)^2\) is \(25\) rather than \(-25\), and the bottom is \(-5+12\) rather than \(-5-12\).

blocks.x: The distributive property turns \(a(b+c)\) into \(ab+ac\). This lesson runs that rule backward. Reading \(ab+ac\) as \(a(b+c)\) is called factoring, and the first problems are pure arithmetic, with no letters in them at all.
Compute \(57\cdot 69+57\cdot 31\) without working out either product. Both terms contain the factor \(57\), so pull it out front and see what the leftover sum becomes.
hints: The first term is \(57\) copies of \(69\), and the second is \(57\) more copies of \(31\). Count copies before multiplying anything.
blocks.sol: Both terms share \(57\), so pull it out front. $$57\cdot 69+57\cdot 31=57(69+31)=57\cdot 100=\boxed{5700}.$$ Counting copies beats multiplying here, since the leftovers add to a round \(100\).

blocks.x: Factoring. Reading \(ab+ac\) as \(a(b+c)\) is called factoring, the distributive property read right to left. Expanding opens parentheses, factoring builds them, and both moves use the same equality. The rewrite is worth having because a shared factor collapses a sum of products into a single product. That is what turned the last problem into a one-step computation, \(57\) copies of \(69\) plus \(57\) copies of \(31\) making \(57\) copies of \(100\).
Compute \(58\cdot 91-58\cdot 81\) the same way. The shared factor comes out front, and this time a subtraction is left behind it. What is the value of the whole expression?
hints: The first product is \(58\) copies of \(91\) and the second is \(58\) copies of \(81\), so subtracting leaves \(58\) copies of some difference.
blocks.sol: Pull the shared \(58\) out front and the subtraction stays inside. $$58\cdot 91-58\cdot 81=58(91-81)=58\cdot 10=\boxed{580}.$$ The long way, \(5278-4698\), reaches the same \(580\) with far more work.

blocks.x: The round trip. The subtraction form \(ab-ac=a(b-c)\) is not a second law, since 1.3 made subtracting \(c\) the same as adding \(-c\). The habit this lesson runs on is checking. Expand every proposed factoring back, and since 2.1 already made you fluent at expanding, you can always grade your own work. The match must be exact, every term and every sign, or the factoring is wrong. The slip it catches most often is dividing only the first term by the shared factor, and one expansion exposes that immediately.

blocks.cap: Two readings of one equality. Expanding opens the parentheses and factoring rebuilds them, so \(3(y+8)\) and \(3y+24\) are the same value written two ways. Below, twenty loose tiles become four equal groups of \(2+3\), which is what \(4(2+3)\) records.

Letters change nothing. The expression \(4w+36\) factors as \(4(w+c)\) for one constant \(c\). Divide each term by the shared \(4\), then enter \(c\).
hints: Both terms get divided by the \(4\), not just the first one.
blocks.sol: Divide both terms by \(4\). Since \(4w\div 4=w\) and \(36\div 4=9\), the factoring is \(4(w+9)\), so \(c=\boxed{9}\). Expanding \(4(w+9)\) lands back on \(4w+36\). Dividing only the first term gives \(4(w+36)\), which expands to \(4w+144\) instead.

blocks.x: How to factor. Find a factor shared by every term, divide each term by it, and write the leftovers inside the parentheses. Each leftover keeps the sign of the term it came from, so a negative term leaves a negative leftover. Finding the shared factor means scanning each term's factors, the parts vocabulary from 1.4, and looking for one that shows up in every term. Then expand your answer, and it has to reproduce the original exactly.

Dana factors \(12h+30\) as \(2(6h+15)\), and expanding it back checks out. But inside the parentheses, \(6h\) and \(15\) still share a factor, so the job is unfinished. Enter the largest number that divides both \(12h\) and \(30\).
hints: What is the largest number that divides both \(12\) and \(30\)?
blocks.sol: Since \(\gcd(12,30)=6\), the largest number dividing both terms is \(\boxed{6}\), and the complete factoring is \(6(2h+5)\). Dana's \(2(6h+15)\) expands back correctly, so passing the round trip does not mean the job is finished. Check whether the leftovers still share a factor.

blocks.x: Factor completely. A partial factoring like \(2(6h+15)\) passes the round trip, since it really does equal \(12h+30\), so completeness needs its own check. Look at the leftovers inside the parentheses, and if they still share a factor bigger than \(1\), pull it out too. An expression is factored completely once the leftovers share nothing but \(1\). The number part of the largest common factor is the GCD from Prealgebra 3.5, which is why \(\gcd(12,30)=6\) finished the job in one pull as \(6(2h+5)\).
A letter can be the shared factor. Since \(y^2\) means \(y\cdot y\) (1.5), both terms of \(y^2+10y\) contain \(y\), so the expression factors as \(y(y+c)\). Enter \(c\).
hints: Divide each term by \(y\) and see what each one leaves behind.
blocks.sol: Divide each term by \(y\). Since \(y^2\div y=y\) and \(10y\div y=10\), the factoring is \(y(y+10)\), and the round trip \(y(y+10)=y^2+10y\) confirms \(c=\boxed{10}\). The terms share no number bigger than \(1\), but a shared letter is a common factor too.

blocks.x: Number and letter combine. Enter the greatest common factor of the two terms of \(8t^2+20t\), typed like a term, for example \(6z\).
hints: Find the number part and the letter part separately, then put them together.
blocks.sol: The number part is \(\gcd(8,20)=4\), and both terms contain one \(t\), so the greatest common factor is \(\boxed{4t}\). Pulling it out gives \(4t(2t+5)\). Answering just \(4\) or just \(t\) stops halfway, since the shared factor carries a number and a letter.

blocks.x: The full scan. The greatest common factor of a set of terms collects two things, the GCD of the number parts and every letter all the terms share. Pulling \(4t\) out of \(8t^2+20t\) leaves \(2t+5\), and since \(2t\) and \(5\) share nothing but \(1\), the factoring is complete. One expansion, \(4t(2t+5)=8t^2+20t\), confirms the whole thing in a line.
A student factors \(8n+36\) as \(4(2n+8)\). Test it the 1.4 way, evaluate the original and the claimed factoring at \(n=1\), each on its own. How far apart are their values?
hints: Work out each expression at \(n=1\) separately, then subtract the results.
blocks.sol: At \(n=1\) the original gives \(8+36=44\) and the claimed factoring gives \(4(2+8)=40\), so the two are \(\boxed{4}\) apart. Expanding catches it faster, since \(4(2n+8)=8n+32\) rather than \(8n+36\). The \(4\) does divide both terms, but the leftover constant is wrong.

blocks.x: Always check by expanding. A wrong factoring cannot pass the round trip, and by 1.4's one-mismatch rule it cannot even survive a single evaluation, since one input giving two different outputs proves the claim false. Expanding is the stronger check and usually the faster one, one distribution compared against the original, term by term and sign by sign. Check every factoring, every time. It costs five seconds and catches everything.
Three terms this time. The expression \(9a+27b-18\) factors as \(9(a+3b+c)\), and each term keeps its sign as the \(9\) comes out. Enter \(c\), sign included.
hints: What is \(-18\) divided by \(9\), sign and all?
blocks.sol: The third term is \(-18\), and \(-18\div 9=-2\), so \(9a+27b-18=9(a+3b-2)\) and \(c=\boxed{-2}\). Each leftover keeps the sign of the term it came from, so dropping the minus would break the expansion.

blocks.x: In \(m(m-6)+8(m-6)\), both terms contain the whole factor \(m-6\). Pull the chunk out front exactly the way the \(57\) came out in this lesson's first problem. The result is \((m+a)(m-6)\). Enter \(a\).
hints: Treat \(m-6\) as a single object, like the shared \(57\) in the hook problem.
The first term is \(m\) copies of \(m-6\), and the second term adds some more copies of the same thing. Count the total number of copies.
blocks.sol: Treat \(m-6\) as one object. The first term is \(m\) copies of it and the second is \(8\) copies, which is \(m+8\) copies in all, so the expression equals \((m+8)(m-6)\) and \(a=\boxed{8}\). Expanding the two products into four separate terms first would erase the shared chunk, and chapter 9 factors quadratics with this same move.

blocks.label: Fun fact
blocks.x: The padlock in your browser's address bar rests on factoring being hard. Multiplying two enormous primes takes a computer an instant, but recovering them from the product alone would outlast the age of the universe.

Factoring reads distribution backward, the round trip checks it, completeness finishes it, and even a whole parenthesized chunk can be the shared factor. Next, 2.4 adds and subtracts entire expressions, and the full sign flip from distributing \(-1\) in 2.1 becomes the main skill.

review.x: Compute \(34\cdot 67+34\cdot 33\) without working out either product. Factor out the shared \(34\) first and see what sum is left behind it.
hints: The sum left behind the \(34\) is \(67+33\), a friendly number.
review.sol: Both terms contain \(34\), so the sum is \(34(67+33)=34\cdot 100=\boxed{3400}\). Grinding out \(2278+1122\) gets there too, just slowly.

review.x: Compute \(76\cdot 53-76\cdot 43\) by factoring first. Both products are ugly, but the difference left behind the shared factor is not.
hints: Pull the \(76\) out front and subtract inside the parentheses.
review.sol: Pull the shared \(76\) out front, since \(76(53-43)=76\cdot 10=\boxed{760}\). Subtracting inside the parentheses is far less work than computing \(4028-3268\).

review.x: The expression \(5q+60\) factors as \(5(q+c)\) for one constant \(c\). Divide each term by the shared \(5\), then enter \(c\).
hints: Divide each term by \(5\), the second one included.
review.sol: Divide each term by \(5\). Since \(5q\div 5=q\) and \(60\div 5=12\), the factoring is \(5(q+12)\), which expands back to \(5q+60\), so \(c=\boxed{12}\). Writing \(5(q+60)\) divides only the first term and fails the round trip.

review.x: Enter the largest number that divides both terms of \(38x+95\). Neither number is small, so factor each one before searching for what they share.
hints: Both \(38\) and \(95\) are a prime times a small number.
review.sol: Since \(38=2\cdot 19\) and \(95=5\cdot 19\), the largest common factor is \(\boxed{19}\) and the complete form is \(19(2x+5)\). Guessing small divisors stalls here, since \(2\) misses \(95\) and \(5\) misses \(38\). Factor each number first instead.

review.x: Ravi factors \(44h+66\) as \(11(4h+6)\), and the expansion checks out. Even so, \(4h\) and \(6\) still share a factor, so the factoring is not complete. Enter the largest common factor of the two original terms.
hints: Passing the round trip is not the same as being finished. Look at what \(4h\) and \(6\) still share.
review.sol: Since \(\gcd(44,66)=22\), the largest common factor is \(\boxed{22}\), and the complete form \(22(2h+3)\) expands back to \(44h+66\). Ravi's \(11(4h+6)\) also expands correctly, but its leftovers \(4h\) and \(6\) still share \(2\), so it is not finished.

review.x: The shared factor is a letter this time. Since \(n^2\) is \(n\cdot n\), both terms of \(n^2+13n\) contain \(n\), so the expression factors as \(n(n+c)\). Enter \(c\).
hints: Divide each term by \(n\).
review.sol: The terms share no number, but both contain \(n\). Dividing each by \(n\) leaves \(n+13\), and the round trip \(n(n+13)=n^2+13n\) confirms \(c=\boxed{13}\).

review.x: Number and letter both matter here. Enter the greatest common factor of the two terms of \(15u^2+25u\), typed like a term, for example \(8w\).
hints: The number part comes from \(15\) and \(25\), and the letter part from what both terms share.
review.sol: The number part is \(\gcd(15,25)=5\), and both terms contain \(u\), so the greatest common factor is \(\boxed{5u}\). Pulling it out gives \(5u(3u+5)\). Entering only \(5\) or only \(u\) stops halfway.

review.x: The expression \(26x+39y-52\) factors as \(13(2x+3y+e)\). Enter \(e\), sign included.
hints: Divide the last term by \(13\), sign and all.
review.sol: Since \(-52\div 13=-4\), the factoring is \(13(2x+3y-4)\), which expands back to \(26x+39y-52\), so \(e=\boxed{-4}\). Each leftover keeps the sign of its own term, so dropping the minus changes the expression.

review.x: Evaluate \(\dfrac{7\cdot 93+7\cdot 7}{10}\) without any long multiplication. The top is a sum of two products with a shared factor, so factor it before dividing anything.
hints: The top is \(7\) copies of a friendly sum.
review.sol: Factor the top first, since \(7\cdot 93+7\cdot 7=7(93+7)=7\cdot 100=700\), and \(700\div 10=\boxed{70}\). The shared \(7\) turns two ugly products into one round number.

review.x: Both terms of \(d(d+5)+3(d+5)\) contain the whole chunk \(d+5\), so it can come out front like any shared factor. Factoring it out gives \((d+a)(d+5)\). Enter \(a\).
hints: Count copies of \(d+5\), treating the chunk as a single object.
review.sol: Count copies of the chunk \(d+5\). The first term is \(d\) copies and the second is \(3\) more, so there are \(d+3\) copies in all, giving \((d+3)(d+5)\) and \(a=\boxed{3}\). The tempting answer \(5\) sits inside the shared chunk, not in the leftover factor.

review.x: One more full scan, this one on \(6t^2+9t\). Enter the greatest common factor of its two terms, typed like a term. Check that the leftovers share nothing before you commit.
hints: Find the number part first, then bring along the letter both terms share.
review.sol: Since \(\gcd(6,9)=3\) and both terms contain \(t\), the greatest common factor is \(\boxed{3t}\) and the complete form is \(3t(2t+3)\). The leftovers \(2t\) and \(3\) share only \(1\), so nothing is left to pull. Stopping at \(3\) would leave the shared \(t\) behind.

review.x: Evaluate \(41^2+41\) by factoring before you compute anything. Done right, one clean product replaces a square plus an addition.
hints: Both terms contain \(41\), since \(41^2\) means \(41\cdot 41\).
After the \(41\) comes out, the parentheses hold \(41+1\).
review.sol: Both terms contain \(41\), so \(41^2+41=41(41+1)=41\cdot 42=\boxed{1722}\). The shape is general, since \(n^2+n\) always factors as \(n(n+1)\), a product of two consecutive whole numbers.

blocks.x: 2.3 said this lesson would add and subtract whole expressions, with the sign flip from distributing \(-1\) as the main skill. That is where it ends up. It starts smaller, with plain counting, because adding expressions begins by counting how many copies of a letter you have.
Start by counting. Nine copies of \(k\) plus four more copies of \(k\) is some number of copies of \(k\), so \(9k+4k=ck\) for a single number \(c\). Enter \(c\).
hints: Count copies and ignore what one copy is worth. Nine of something plus four more of the same thing is how many of it?
blocks.sol: Nine copies plus four more copies is thirteen copies, whatever a copy is worth, so \(9k+4k=13k\) and \(c=\boxed{13}\). Copies add here, they never multiply, so the \(9\) and the \(4\) are added rather than multiplied.

blocks.x: Like terms. Terms with identical variable parts, like \(9k\) and \(4k\), are called like terms, and they combine by adding their coefficients. The reason comes straight from 2.3, and it fits in one line, $$9k+4k=(9+4)k=13k.$$ Combining like terms is factoring, the shared letter is the common factor and the coefficients add behind it, so nothing new is being invented in this lesson. The coefficients do all the arithmetic and the letter rides along unchanged.
Jae simplifies \(7w+3\) to \(10w\). Test the claim the 1.4 way, evaluate both expressions at \(w=2\), each on its own, and enter how far apart the two values are.
hints: One input, two values. Work out \(7w+3\) at \(w=2\), then \(10w\) at \(w=2\), and compare.
blocks.sol: At \(w=2\) the original gives \(14+3=17\) while \(10w\) gives \(20\), so the two values sit \(\boxed{3}\) apart. By 1.4, one input with two different outputs settles it, the claim is false. The merge \(7+3=10\) treated \(7w\) and \(3\) as the same kind of term.

blocks.x: Unlike terms stay apart. Nothing was wrong with \(7w+3\) in the first place. Its terms share no factor to pull out, so no combining is possible and the expression was already finished. The split is not just letters against numbers, since 1.5 makes \(x^2\) mean \(x\cdot x\), a different factor structure from \(x\), so \(x^2\) and \(x\) are unlike as well. Simplified does not mean one term. It means every family has been collected exactly once.

blocks.cap: On top, each family collects on its own, so the \(x\) terms give \(5x\) and the plain numbers give \(8\), and nothing crosses between them. Below, a minus in front of parentheses multiplies every term inside by \(-1\), so both signs flip. Flipping only the first sign is the error to watch for.

blocks.x: Add two expressions. \((5d+9)+(2d+8)\) simplifies to one \(d\) term plus one constant. Enter the constant term of the result.
hints: In a pure sum the parentheses change nothing by 1.3, so drop them and collect each family on its own.
blocks.sol: Drop the parentheses and the sum is \(5d+9+2d+8\). The \(d\) family collects to \(7d\) and the constants to \(9+8=17\), so the result is \(7d+17\) and the constant term is \(\boxed{17}\). Piling all four numbers into one total would be wrong, since \(5d\) and \(9\) are unlike.

blocks.x: Adding expressions. In a pure sum the parentheses do nothing, since 1.3 lets addition regroup and reorder freely, so \((5d+9)+(2d+8)\) is just the four terms \(5d+9+2d+8\) taken in whatever order helps. Drop the parentheses, then sweep family by family, every \(d\) term into one total, every constant into another, and write the totals side by side.
Now subtract. \((9p+7)-(4p+3)\) simplifies to one \(p\) term plus one constant. Enter the coefficient of \(p\) in the result.
hints: The minus applies to the whole second expression, so both \(4p\) and \(3\) get subtracted.
blocks.sol: The \(p\) terms give \(9p-4p=5p\) and the constants give \(7-3=4\), so the result is \(5p+4\) and the coefficient of \(p\) is \(\boxed{5}\). The minus applies to the whole second expression. Flipping only the first sign gives \(9p+7-4p+3=5p+10\), which adds the \(3\) instead of subtracting it.

blocks.x: Simplify \((11h+9)-(7h-5)\). The expression being subtracted carries a minus of its own this time. Enter the constant term of the simplified result.
hints: Rewrite the subtraction first. Distribute \(-1\) over the whole second expression, the 2.1 move.
After the rewrite, check what happened to the \(-5\). What sign does it carry when the constants collect?
blocks.sol: The minus multiplies every term of \(7h-5\) by \(-1\), so the expression becomes \(11h+9-7h+5\). The \(h\) family gives \(4h\) and the constants give \(9+5=\boxed{14}\). Flipping only the first sign leaves \(11h+9-7h-5\) and a constant of \(4\), the classic error.

blocks.x: Subtracting is distributing \(-1\). A minus in front of parentheses is multiplication by \(-1\), the rule from 2.1, so subtracting an expression multiplies every one of its terms by \(-1\) and then everything adds. In practice, flip every sign of the expression being subtracted, write the flipped line down, then sweep family by family as usual. The most common simplification error in all of algebra flips only the first sign, and writing the fully flipped line before collecting anything is the habit that kills it.
Simplify \((7u+12)-(7u+4)\) completely, flipping both signs of the second expression first. The result is shorter than usual. Enter the single number that remains.
hints: Run the sweep and watch what the \(u\) family adds up to.
blocks.sol: Flipping both signs gives \(7u+12-7u-4\). The \(u\) family totals \(7u-7u=0u\) and drops out entirely, and the constants give \(12-4=8\), so the whole expression is \(\boxed{8}\). Flipping only the first sign would leave \(+4\) and a total of \(16\).

blocks.x: Families can vanish. A family can total zero copies and drop out of the answer entirely, the way \(7u-7u\) just did, leaving only a plain number behind. The constants can vanish the same way, leaving a pure variable term. Zero copies of anything is nothing, so write nothing, not \(0u\). A long expression collapsing to something tiny is not a mistake, it is exactly what the sweep is for, and it happens constantly once equations arrive in chapter 4.
Two letters now. Simplify \((4a+9b)+(6a-2b)\). The \(a\) terms and the \(b\) terms collect separately. Enter the coefficient of \(b\) in the result.
hints: Each letter is its own family, one sweep for the \(a\) terms and a separate sweep for the \(b\) terms.
blocks.sol: One sweep per letter. The \(a\) family gives \(4a+6a=10a\), the \(b\) family gives \(9b-2b=7b\), and the two totals never mix, so the result is \(10a+7b\). The \(10\) belongs to \(a\), and the coefficient of \(b\) is \(\boxed{7}\).

blocks.x: Three expressions chained together. Simplify \((2t-5)+(6-3t)+(4t+1)\). The constants sit in a different spot inside each pair of parentheses. Enter the constant term of the result.
hints: One sweep per family, and 1.3 says the order the terms arrive in does not matter.
blocks.sol: The \(t\) family gives \(2t-3t+4t=3t\) and the constants give \(-5+6+1=2\), so the result is \(3t+2\) and the constant term is \(\boxed{2}\). Where a constant sits inside its parentheses changes nothing, and the \(3\) is the coefficient, not the ask.

blocks.x: One sweep per family. However many expressions are chained together, one sweep per family finishes the job, and a written running total for each family, the 2.2 habit of putting middle steps on paper, is what keeps the signs honest. Two notes for the practice ahead. A family's total can come out negative, and that minus stays glued to the coefficient in the answer. And a bare letter counts as one copy, \(r\) means \(1r\), so it joins its family's count like any other term.
The whole chapter in one line. Expand \(k(k+9)\) with 2.1, then simplify \(k(k+9)-k^2\) completely. One family remains. Enter the coefficient of \(k\).
hints: Expand first. 2.1 turns \(k(k+9)\) into two terms.
After expanding, decide which terms are actually like. 1.5 says \(k^2\) and \(k\) are different families.
blocks.sol: Expanding gives \(k^2+9k-k^2\). The only like pair is \(k^2-k^2\), which vanishes, leaving \(9k\), so the coefficient of \(k\) is \(\boxed{9}\). Combining \(k^2\) with \(9k\) is tempting, but 1.5 makes them different families.

blocks.label: Fun fact
blocks.x: Chapter 14 adds and subtracts entire polynomials, expressions carrying a dozen terms or more at once, and every bit of that work is this lesson's family-by-family sweep run at a bigger scale.

Expressions now add, subtract, expand, and factor, four moves resting on the same handful of chapter 1 rules, and all of it reduces to counting copies and flipping signs. Next, 2.5 turns to fractions whose tops and bottoms hold variables, and the same care with rewriting carries straight over.

review.x: Twelve copies of \(g\) plus six more copies is some number of copies of \(g\). Write \(12g+6g\) as a single term \(cg\) and enter \(c\).
hints: Count copies of \(g\), the way you would count any objects.
review.sol: Twelve copies of \(g\) plus six more is eighteen copies, so \(12g+6g=18g\) and \(c=\boxed{18}\). Addition counts copies rather than multiplying them, so the \(72\) from multiplying the coefficients is not it.

review.x: A student simplifies \(8y+1\) to \(9y\). Settle it the 1.4 way. Evaluate both expressions at \(y=5\), each on its own, and enter how far apart their values are.
hints: One input, two values. Substitute \(y=5\) into each expression separately.
review.sol: At \(y=5\) the original gives \(40+1=41\) while \(9y\) gives \(45\), so the gap is \(45-41=\boxed{4}\). One mismatch proves the claim false. The merge \(8+1=9\) treated the unlike terms \(8y\) and \(1\) as like.

review.x: Two expressions added. Simplify \((3c+10)+(8c+5)\) down to one \(c\) term plus one constant, and enter the constant term of the simplified result.
hints: In a pure sum the parentheses drop. Then collect family by family.
review.sol: The parentheses drop and each family collects, \(3c+8c=11c\) and \(10+5=15\), so the result is \(11c+15\) and the constant term is \(\boxed{15}\). Entering \(11\) names the coefficient instead of the constant.

review.x: Now a subtraction. Simplify \((12v+11)-(8v+1)\) down to one \(v\) term plus one constant, and enter the constant term of the simplified result.
hints: The minus reaches both terms of \((8v+1)\), not just the \(8v\).
review.sol: The minus multiplies both terms of \((8v+1)\), so the expression becomes \(12v+11-8v-1\) and the constants give \(11-1=\boxed{10}\). Flipping only the first sign leaves \(+1\) and a constant of \(12\).

review.x: Simplify \((9s+4)-(3s-7)\) down to one \(s\) term plus one constant, and enter the constant term of the simplified result.
hints: What does the minus in front of \((3s-7)\) do to the \(-7\)?
review.sol: The minus multiplies every term of \((3s-7)\), so the \(-7\) becomes \(+7\) and the constants give \(4+7=\boxed{11}\). Flipping only the first sign gives \(9s+4-3s-7\) and a constant of \(-3\).

review.x: Simplify \((5x+20)-(5x+14)\) completely and enter the single number that remains. Distribute the minus first, then total each family.
hints: Watch what the \(x\) family adds up to before writing the result.
review.sol: Distributing the minus gives \(5x+20-5x-14\). The \(x\) family totals \(5-5=0\) copies and vanishes, so all that remains is \(20-14=\boxed{6}\). Zero copies of \(x\) is nothing at all. Flipping only the first sign would land on \(34\).

review.x: Two letters and a subtraction. Simplify \((5a+6b)-(3a+13b)\) and enter the coefficient of \(b\) in the simplified result, sign included.
hints: A family's total can come out negative. Track the sign of the \(b\) sweep.
review.sol: Distributing the minus makes the \(b\) family \(6b-13b=-7b\), so the coefficient of \(b\) is \(\boxed{-7}\). The minus stays glued to the coefficient. Flipping only the first sign leaves \(+13b\) and a total of \(19\).

review.x: Three expressions chained. Simplify \((6n+11)+(n-15)+(2n+4)\) with one sweep per family, then enter the constant term of the simplified result.
hints: The bare \(n\) counts as one copy, \(1n\).
review.sol: Every parenthesis drops in a pure sum, and the constants collect to \(11-15+4=\boxed{0}\). The bare \(n\) counts as one copy, which makes the \(n\) family \(6+1+2=9\), but \(9\) is the coefficient, not the constant.

review.x: Simplify \((3x^2+8x)+(9x^2-2x)\) and enter the coefficient of \(x^2\) in the simplified result. Keep each family separate as you collect.
hints: \(x^2\) and \(x\) are separate families by 1.5. Collect each on its own.
review.sol: The \(x^2\) family gives \(3+9=12\) and the \(x\) family gives \(8-2=6\), so the result is \(12x^2+6x\) and the coefficient of \(x^2\) is \(\boxed{12}\). Adding all four coefficients to \(18\) treats \(x^2\) and \(x\) as one family, and their factor structures differ.

review.x: Simplify first, then evaluate. Reduce \((6q+10)-(4q-3)\) to one \(q\) term plus one constant, then evaluate the simplified result at \(q=4\) and enter the value.
hints: Simplify before substituting. It turns the evaluation into one small step.
review.sol: Subtracting the whole quantity flips the \(-3\) to \(+3\), so the simplified form is \(2q+13\), and at \(q=4\) the value is \(8+13=\boxed{21}\). Flipping only the first sign gives \(2q+7\) and a value of \(15\).

review.x: Expand, then combine. Rewrite \(4(r+8)-r\) with the parentheses gone, collect the \(r\) family, and enter the constant term of the simplified result.
hints: Distribute the \(4\) over both inside terms before touching the \(-r\).
review.sol: The \(4\) multiplies both inside terms, so \(4(r+8)-r\) becomes \(4r+32-r=3r+32\) and the constant term is \(\boxed{32}\). Distributing onto the \(r\) alone gives \(4r+8-r\) and a constant of \(8\), the 2.1 partial-expansion error.

review.x: Three expressions, one subtraction. Simplify \((5z+16)+(7z-6)-(12z+9)\) completely and enter the single number that remains.
hints: Rewrite the subtraction by distributing the minus over both terms of \((12z+9)\) first.
Then run one sweep per family, the \(z\) terms in one pass and the constants in another.
review.sol: Distributing the minus gives \(5z+16+7z-6-12z-9\). The \(z\) family totals \(5+7-12=0\) and vanishes, and the constants total \(16-6-9=1\), so what remains is \(\boxed{1}\). A check at \(z=2\) gives \(26+8-33=1\). Flipping only the first sign of the last expression would keep the \(+9\) and give \(19\).

blocks.x: Now the tops and bottoms of fractions hold variables. A fraction bar is division, and a letter on the top or bottom is just an unknown number, so none of the fraction arithmetic from prealgebra changes. The care with signs from 2.4 carries straight over too.

A letter is just an unknown number. Every fraction rule from prealgebra still holds with a letter in the mix, making an equivalent fraction by multiplying top and bottom by the same thing, finding a common denominator, reducing to lowest terms. None of them ever needed the actual value. This is the same number arithmetic you already know, with a letter standing in for a value we have not been told.
Combine \(\frac{2}{c}+\frac{5}{c}\) into a single fraction over \(c\). Enter the numerator.
hints: The bottoms already match, so you are just counting pieces of size \(\frac{1}{c}\).
blocks.sol: The bottoms already match, so just count the pieces, \(2+5=\boxed{7}\), giving \(\frac{7}{c}\). The bottom stays \(c\). Gathering more pieces of one size does not change the size of a piece.

blocks.x: Same bottom, add the tops. The denominator names the size of each piece, so two copies of \(\frac{1}{x}\) plus five more copies is seven of them, \(\frac{2}{x}+\frac{5}{x}=\frac{7}{x}\). This is the counting of like things from 2.4, the shared bottom plays the role of the shared letter and the numerators add in front of it. The bottom is left alone, because gathering more pieces of one size does not change the size of a piece.
Write \(\frac{9m+8}{7}-\frac{4m-3}{7}\) as one fraction over \(7\). Enter the constant term of the numerator.
hints: Subtracting the whole top subtracts both of its terms, the sign-flip from 2.4.
blocks.sol: The minus hits every term of \(4m-3\), so the top is \(9m+8-4m+3=5m+11\) and the constant is \(\boxed{11}\). Drop the flip on the \(-3\) and you get \(5\) instead, which is the usual slip.

blocks.x: Reducing means dividing top and bottom by the same nonzero factor. To write a fraction in lowest terms you divide the top and the bottom by a common factor, exactly as with numbers. With a variable in the mix you often cannot see that common factor until you factor first, the 2.3 move, so pull the shared factor out of the top and the bottom, then divide it away. The factor you cancel has to be nonzero, which every common factor here is.

blocks.cap: Both routes start from a fraction sharing a piece top and bottom. Up top the \(20\) is a factor, it multiplies the whole numerator and the whole denominator, so dividing both by \(20\) is legal. Below, the \(u\) is only a term inside \(u+14\), so crossing it out changes the value. A factor is a whole multiplied chunk, a term is one piece of a sum, and only factors cancel.

blocks.x: Simplify \(\frac{6n+15}{3}\) by factoring the top and cancelling, then evaluate the result at \(n=4\). Enter the value.
hints: Factor the top before cancelling. What divides both \(6n\) and \(15\)?
blocks.sol: Factor the top, \(\frac{3(2n+5)}{3}=2n+5\), and at \(n=4\) that is \(8+5=\boxed{13}\). Cancelling the \(3\) against only the \(15\) is the slip. The \(3\) has to divide the whole top before it can go.

blocks.x: A classmate simplifies \(\frac{r+10}{r}\) to \(10\) by crossing out the \(r\)'s. Test the original \(\frac{r+10}{r}\) at \(r=2\), the 1.4 way. Enter its value.
hints: Evaluate the untouched fraction and compare with the \(10\) the cancel claims.
blocks.sol: At \(r=2\) the untouched fraction is \(\frac{2+10}{2}=\frac{12}{2}=\boxed{6}\), not the \(10\) the cancel claims. Here \(r\) is a term of \(r+10\), not a factor of the whole top, so crossing it out is illegal.

blocks.x: Only a whole factor cancels. A factor is a chunk that multiplies the entire top and the entire bottom. A term is just one piece of a sum. You may divide away a shared factor, but you may never cross out a single term, because a lone term is not multiplying the whole thing. The evaluation just above shows why. Crossing out the \(r\) gave \(10\), while the real value was \(6\), so the illegal cut changed the number. Factor first, then cancel only what multiplies the whole top and bottom.
Simplify \(\frac{8b-40}{b-5}\). Factor the top, cancel the shared \((b-5)\), and enter what is left.
hints: Nothing cancels until the top is factored. Pull the common factor out of \(8b-40\).
blocks.sol: Factor the top, \(\frac{8(b-5)}{b-5}\). The whole chunk \((b-5)\) is shared, so it divides out and leaves \(\boxed{8}\). Nothing cancels until the top is factored, since a loose piece of a sum is not a factor.

blocks.x: Add \(\frac{3}{p}+\frac{7}{4p}\) over the common denominator \(4p\). Enter the numerator.
hints: \(4p\) is a multiple of \(p\). Scale \(\frac{3}{p}\) up by \(\frac{4}{4}\), an equivalent fraction.
blocks.sol: Scale the first fraction, \(\frac{3}{p}=\frac{12}{4p}\), then add over \(4p\), \(12+7=\boxed{19}\). Adding \(3+7\) straight across skips the scaling, and the pieces are different sizes until you do it.

blocks.x: No shared factor, use the product. When two bottoms share no common factor, their product is always a common denominator. Scale each fraction up to it, the first fraction by the second bottom and the second fraction by the first, top and bottom by the same thing so each stays an equivalent fraction. Then the two bottoms match and you combine the tops.
Write \(\frac{3v+2}{4}-\frac{v-7}{3}\) as one fraction over \(12\). Enter the constant term of the numerator.
hints: The bottoms \(4\) and \(3\) share no factor, so \(12\) is their product.
Scale each fraction to twelfths, then subtract the whole second top.
blocks.sol: Over \(12\) the tops are \(3(3v+2)=9v+6\) and \(4(v-7)=4v-28\). The minus takes the whole second top, \(9v+6-4v+28=5v+34\), so the constant is \(\boxed{34}\). Miss the flip on the \(-28\) and you land at \(-22\).

blocks.x: Subtracting subtracts the whole top. A subtraction sign in front of a fraction takes away the entire numerator, so once the bottoms match, every sign in that top flips. It is the same \(-1\) spread over every term you saw in 2.4, now in fraction form. Miss one sign and the constant comes out wrong. A sum or difference rewritten as a single fraction in lowest terms is the finished form, one bar, one top, one bottom.
Combine \(\frac{5f+15}{f+3}-\frac{2}{f}\) into a single fraction of the form \(\frac{5f+k}{f}\). Enter \(k\) (typed like -7).
hints: Cancel the \((f+3)\) chunk in the first fraction first.
Then write \(5\) as \(\frac{5f}{f}\) to subtract the \(\frac{2}{f}\).
blocks.sol: Cancel the shared chunk, \(\frac{5(f+3)}{f+3}=5\), then \(5-\frac{2}{f}=\frac{5f-2}{f}\), so \(k=\boxed{-2}\). Writing \(5\) as \(\frac{5f}{f}\) is what makes the subtraction possible. \(5-\frac{2}{f}\) is not \(\frac{3}{f}\).

blocks.x: Fact. Cancel only a factor shared by the whole top and the whole bottom. A single term of a sum never cancels, no matter how much it looks like the number below it.

Every fraction here had a single letter in it. 2.6 puts several letters in one expression at once. The counting of like pieces and the care with signs work exactly the same way with more letters to track, so the rewrites you just practiced are already the whole toolkit.

review.x: Add \(\frac{4}{g}+\frac{5}{g}\). Enter the numerator of the sum over \(g\).
hints: The bottoms already match, so you are just counting pieces of size \(\frac{1}{g}\).
review.sol: The bottoms already match, so count the pieces, \(4+5=\boxed{9}\). The bottom stays \(g\). Adding the bottoms too is the common slip, but gathering more pieces of one size does not change the size of a piece.

review.x: Combine \(\frac{8k-3}{5}-\frac{8k-7}{5}\) over \(5\). Enter the numerator.
hints: Subtracting the whole top flips both of its signs, the sign-flip from 2.4.
review.sol: The minus hits every term of \(8k-7\), so \(8k-3-8k+7=\boxed{4}\). Half-flipping to \(8k-3-8k-7\) lands the constant at \(-10\), so flip both signs of the second top.

review.x: Simplify \(\frac{10e+35}{5}\) by factoring the top and cancelling, then evaluate the result at \(e=3\). Enter the value.
hints: Factor the top before cancelling. What divides both \(10e\) and \(35\)?
review.sol: Factor the top, \(\frac{5(2e+7)}{5}=2e+7\), and at \(e=3\) that is \(6+7=\boxed{13}\). Cancelling the \(5\) against only the \(35\) is the slip. The \(5\) has to divide the whole top before it can go.

review.x: A student cancels the \(h\)'s in \(\frac{h+15}{h}\) and writes \(15\). Evaluate the original \(\frac{h+15}{h}\) at \(h=3\), the 1.4 way, and enter the true value.
hints: Evaluate the untouched fraction and compare it with the \(15\) the cancel claims.
review.sol: At \(h=3\) the untouched fraction is \(\frac{3+15}{3}=\frac{18}{3}=\boxed{6}\), not the \(15\) the cancel claims. Here \(h\) is a term of \(h+15\), not a factor of the whole top, so crossing it out is illegal.

review.x: Simplify \(\frac{7c-63}{c-9}\) by factoring the top and cancelling \((c-9)\). Enter what is left.
hints: Nothing cancels until the top is factored. Pull the common factor out of \(7c-63\).
review.sol: Factor the top, \(\frac{7(c-9)}{c-9}\). The whole chunk \((c-9)\) is shared, so it divides out and leaves \(\boxed{7}\). Nothing cancels until the top is factored, since a loose piece of a sum is not a factor.

review.x: Simplify \(\frac{10(x-3)}{4(x-3)}\) by cancelling the shared \((x-3)\). Enter the number left, in lowest terms.
hints: The whole chunk \((x-3)\) divides out top and bottom. What number fraction is left?
review.sol: The \((x-3)\) is a whole factor of both, so it divides out and leaves \(\frac{10}{4}=\boxed{\frac{5}{2}}\). Stopping at \(\frac{10}{4}\) is the easy miss. The number part still reduces.

review.x: Add \(\frac{5}{y}+\frac{3}{2y}\). Scale the first to halves-of-\(y\), add over \(2y\), and enter the numerator.
hints: \(2y\) is a multiple of \(y\). Scale \(\frac{5}{y}\) up by \(\frac{2}{2}\), an equivalent fraction.
review.sol: Scale the first fraction, \(\frac{5}{y}=\frac{10}{2y}\), then add over \(2y\), \(10+3=\boxed{13}\). Adding \(5+3\) straight across skips the scaling, and the pieces are different sizes until you do it.

review.x: The denominators of \(\frac{4}{j}+\frac{7}{k}\) share no factor. Enter their least common denominator, typed like \(jk\).
hints: When two bottoms have no common factor, their product is a common denominator.
review.sol: With no shared factor, the product of the bottoms works, so the least common denominator is \(\boxed{jk}\). Neither \(j\) nor \(k\) divides the other, so neither one alone can serve as a common bottom.

review.x: Combine \(\frac{r+3}{2}-\frac{r-8}{5}\) over \(10\). The subtraction flips every sign of the second top. Enter the constant term of the combined numerator.
hints: The bottoms \(2\) and \(5\) share no factor, so \(10\) is their product.
Scale each fraction to tenths, then subtract the whole second top, flipping its signs, the 2.4 move.
review.sol: Over \(10\) the tops are \(5(r+3)=5r+15\) and \(2(r-8)=2r-16\). The minus takes the whole second top, \(5r+15-2r+16=3r+31\), so the constant is \(\boxed{31}\). Miss the flip on the \(-16\) and you land at \(-1\).

review.x: In \(\frac{4x+9}{x}\) a student cancels the \(x\) from \(4x\) against the bottom and writes \(13\). Evaluate the original at \(x=3\) and enter the true value.
hints: The \(x\) in \(4x\) is tied into a term of the sum, not a factor of the whole top. Evaluate the untouched fraction.
review.sol: Keep the fraction whole and substitute. At \(x=3\) it is \(\frac{4(3)+9}{3}=\frac{21}{3}=\boxed{7}\), not the \(13\) the cancel claims. The \(x\) in \(4x\) is tied into one term of \(4x+9\), so it is not a factor of the whole top.

review.x: Combine \(\frac{4s-3}{6}-\frac{2s-6}{3}\) into one fraction and reduce. The \(s\) terms cancel. Enter the result in lowest terms.
hints: Scale the second fraction to sixths, then subtract the whole top, flipping its signs, the 2.4 move.
After the flip the \(4s\) terms cancel, leaving a pure number fraction to reduce.
review.sol: Scale the second fraction to sixths, \(\frac{2s-6}{3}=\frac{4s-12}{6}\). The minus takes the whole top, \((4s-3)-(4s-12)=9\), so the result is \(\frac{9}{6}=\boxed{\frac{3}{2}}\). Half-flipping to \(4s-3-4s-12\) gives \(-15\) instead.

review.x: Simplify \(\frac{12w}{4w}\) and enter that number.
hints: The whole factor \(4w\) divides both top and bottom. What plain number is left?
review.sol: Divide top and bottom by the whole shared factor \(4w\), leaving \(\frac{12}{4}=\boxed{3}\). Cancelling only the \(w\) and stopping at \(\frac{12}{4}\) is the easy miss, since the numbers still reduce.

blocks.x: Everything from 2.5 still works when more than one letter is in view. Take \(8ab+9ab\). The coefficients add the 2.4 way, \(8+9=17\), so \(8ab+9ab=17ab\), and the \(ab\) stays as it is. The one new question is what counts as the same kind of term, now that a single term can carry several letters.
Combine \(7st+6st\) into one term. Type its coefficient.
hints: \(st\) is one variable part, so this is a single family.
Add the coefficients, the 2.4 way.
blocks.sol: \(st\) is one variable part, so the coefficients add, \(7+6=\boxed{13}\). Two letters in a term does not make it two families. The whole variable part is what has to match.

blocks.x: A single term can multiply several letters. Terms like \(ab\), \(2mn\), and \(5rst\) are one term each, a coefficient times a product of letters. Because multiplication reorders freely, the 1.3 move, the order of the letters inside a term does not matter. So \(ab\) and \(ba\) are the same term, and \(mn\) and \(nm\) are the same term.

Like terms match the whole variable part. Two terms are like only when their entire variable part is identical, every letter and its power. So \(4jk\) and \(9jk\) are like and combine to \(13jk\), but \(4jk\) and \(4j\) are unlike, and \(4jk\) and \(4j^2k\) are unlike, since \(j^2\) means \(j\cdot j\), the 1.5 reading. Here is why the whole part has to match. If an illegal merge like \(6ab+4a=10ab\) were true, the two sides would agree at every input, the 1.4 test, and they do not. blocks.cap: Same variable part means the same tile shape, so three \(xy\) tiles stack and their coefficients add to \(3xy\). An \(xy\) tile and an \(xz\) tile are different shapes, so they stay as two separate terms no matter how alike the letters look.

blocks.x: A classmate rewrote \(5cd+5c\) as \(10cd\), adding the coefficients as if the terms matched. Evaluate the original \(5cd+5c\) at \(c=2,\ d=4\). Type the value.
hints: Are \(5cd\) and \(5c\) really like terms? Compare their variable parts.
Put \(c=2,\ d=4\) into the original \(5cd+5c\), one letter at a time.
blocks.sol: Substitute into the original. \(5cd=5\cdot2\cdot4=40\) and \(5c=5\cdot2=10\), so the value is \(40+10=\boxed{50}\). The classmate's \(10cd\) gives \(80\) at the same input, and one input with two different outputs proves \(5cd\) and \(5c\) are unlike.

blocks.x: Combine one family at a time. To simplify, sweep the expression once for each distinct variable part, add the coefficients in that family, and keep the variable part unchanged. This is the 2.4 count with more letters in view. A minus sign belongs to the term right after it, so \(-3wv\) contributes \(-3\) to the \(vw\) family once you use \(wv=vw\) from 1.3.
Simplify \(11mn+9m-5nm\) by combining like terms. Type the coefficient of the \(mn\) term.
hints: \(nm\) is the same variable part as \(mn\), so the order does not matter.
The minus travels with its term into the \(mn\) family; the \(9m\) is a different family.
blocks.sol: Read \(nm\) as \(mn\), so \(11mn-5mn=6mn\), and the \(9m\) is a separate family. The coefficient is \(\boxed{6}\). Order inside a term is free, so a backward-written term still joins its family, and its minus sign comes with it.

blocks.x: A distributed factor reaches every term. When a factor that carries a letter multiplies a sum, it multiplies each term inside, the 2.1 move. So \(2h(3k+4m)=6hk+8hm\), the \(h\) joins both products. If the letter fell off one term, the two expressions would disagree on a test input, so the letter has to travel to every term.
Distribute \(8r(2s+t)\). Type the coefficient of the \(rs\) term.
hints: The \(8r\) multiplies every term inside the parentheses.
You only need the term that has \(r\) and \(s\).
blocks.sol: \(8r\cdot2s=16rs\) and \(8r\cdot t=8rt\), so the \(rs\) coefficient is \(\boxed{16}\). The \(8r\) multiplies both terms inside, not just the first.

blocks.x: Simplify \(2(4uv+5v)+7uv\) by distributing then combining like terms. Type the coefficient of the \(uv\) term.
hints: Distribute the \(2\) across both terms inside first.
Only the \(uv\) terms combine; the plain \(v\) term is a different family.
blocks.sol: Distribute first, \(2(4uv+5v)=8uv+10v\). Only the \(uv\) terms combine, \(8uv+7uv=15uv\), so the coefficient is \(\boxed{15}\). The \(10v\) has a different variable part, so it never joins the \(uv\) count.

blocks.x: Factor out everything shared. The greatest common factor takes the number GCD and every letter that appears in all of the terms, the full scan from 2.3. Pull it to the front, and each leftover keeps its sign. For \(6mn+9mp\) the number GCD is \(3\) and only \(m\) is in both terms, so \(6mn+9mp=3m(2n+3p)\). The \(n\) and \(p\) are not shared, so they stay inside.
Find the greatest common factor of the terms in \(8pqr+12pqs\), typed like \(2xy\), the number first and the letters in alphabetical order.
hints: Take the GCD of \(8\) and \(12\) first.
Which letters appear in BOTH terms? Only those come out front.
blocks.sol: The GCD of \(8\) and \(12\) is \(4\), and \(p\) and \(q\) are the letters sitting in both terms, so the GCF is \(\boxed{4pq}\). The \(r\) and \(s\) each appear in only one term, so neither can come out front.

blocks.x: Substitute one letter at a time. To evaluate a multi-variable expression, replace each letter with its given value, then do the arithmetic, the 1.6 way. A term like \(4mn\) needs both values, \(4\cdot m\cdot n\), so dropping either letter is the common miss. Work one term at a time and the arithmetic stays plain.
Evaluate \(4gh-2g+h\) at \(g=5,\ h=2\). Type the value.
hints: \(4gh\) needs both letters, so \(4\cdot g\cdot h\).
Handle the \(-2g\) and \(+h\) after the \(4gh\) term.
blocks.sol: \(4\cdot5\cdot2=40\), then \(-2\cdot5=-10\) and \(+2\), so \(40-10+2=\boxed{32}\). A term like \(4gh\) needs both values, and reading it as \(4g\) drops the \(h\).

blocks.x: Simplify \(2d(4e+f)+9de\) by distributing and combining, then evaluate the result at \(d=2,\ e=1,\ f=5\). Type the value.
hints: Distribute \(2d\) first, keeping the \(d\) on both new terms.
Combine the \(de\) terms, then substitute \(d=2,\ e=1,\ f=5\).
blocks.sol: Distribute, \(2d(4e+f)=8de+2df\), then combine, \(8de+9de=17de\). Now substitute, \(17\cdot2\cdot1=34\) and \(2\cdot2\cdot5=20\), so \(34+20=\boxed{54}\). The \(d\) has to stay on both new terms, and \(de\) and \(df\) are different families, so they never merge.

blocks.x: Two terms are like only when their whole variable part matches, every letter and its power. A shared coefficient or a single shared letter is not enough, which is why \(4ab\) and \(4a\) never combine.

That caps Chapter 2. Distribute, combine, factor, and evaluate are the whole toolkit, and none of them changed when several letters came into view. Only the like-term rule widened, since the variable part now has to match in full. Chapter 3 turns to exponents, the shorthand for a letter multiplied by itself over and over, along with the rules that come with them.

review.x: Combine \(5jk+9jk\). Type the coefficient.
hints: \(jk\) is a single variable part, so this is one family. Add the coefficients, the 2.4 way.
review.sol: \(jk\) is one variable part, so the coefficients add, \(5+9=\boxed{14}\).

review.x: Combine \(7gh+8hg\). Type the coefficient.
hints: \(hg\) is the same variable part as \(gh\), the order inside is free, the 1.3 move.
review.sol: \(hg\) and \(gh\) are the same variable part, so both terms sit in one family and \(7+8=\boxed{15}\). Flipping the letters inside a term does not make a new family.

review.x: After combining like terms in \(5mp+2m+4mp\), how many terms remain?
hints: Only the \(mp\) terms combine; the \(2m\) is a different family.
review.sol: The \(mp\) family gives \(5+4=9mp\), and \(2m\) stands on its own, so \(\boxed{2}\) terms remain. The \(2m\) has a different variable part, so it never joins the \(mp\) count.

review.x: Are \(6ab\) and \(6a\) like terms? Type yes or no.
hints: Compare the whole variable part, every letter, not just the coefficient.
review.sol: The variable parts are \(ab\) and \(a\), and those differ, so \(\boxed{\text{no}}\). A shared coefficient and one shared letter are not enough, since the whole variable part has to match.

review.x: Evaluate \(4pq+3p\) at \(p=2,\ q=5\). Type the value.
hints: \(4pq\) needs both letters, \(4\cdot p\cdot q\).
review.sol: \(4\cdot2\cdot5=40\) and \(3\cdot2=6\), so \(40+6=\boxed{46}\). The \(4pq\) term needs both values, and reading it as \(4p\) drops the \(q\).

review.x: Evaluate \(2mn+4m-n\) at \(m=3,\ n=1\). Type the value.
hints: \(2mn\) uses both values; handle the \(4m\) and \(-n\) after.
review.sol: \(2\cdot3\cdot1=6\), \(4\cdot3=12\), and the last term is \(-1\), so \(6+12-1=\boxed{17}\). The \(2mn\) term needs both values, not just the \(m\).

review.x: Distribute \(2a(4b+3c)\). Type the coefficient of the \(ab\) term.
hints: The \(2a\) multiplies every term inside; you only need the one with \(a\) and \(b\).
review.sol: \(2a\cdot4b=8ab\), so the \(ab\) coefficient is \(\boxed{8}\). The \(2a\) multiplies both terms inside, not just the first.

review.x: Distribute \(5m(2n+4p)\). Type the coefficient of the \(mp\) term.
hints: The \(5m\) reaches both terms; you only need the one with \(m\) and \(p\).
review.sol: The \(mp\) term comes from \(5m\cdot4p=20mp\), so the coefficient is \(\boxed{20}\). The other product, \(5m\cdot2n=10mn\), is a different family.

review.x: Simplify \(3r(s+2)+4rs\). Type the coefficient of the \(rs\) term.
hints: Distribute the \(3r\) across both terms inside first, the 2.1 move.
The \(3r\cdot2\) gives a plain \(r\) term, a different family from \(rs\).
review.sol: Distribute, \(3r(s+2)=3rs+6r\). Only the \(rs\) terms combine, \(3rs+4rs=7rs\), so the coefficient is \(\boxed{7}\). The \(6r\) has no \(s\), so it stays out of the \(rs\) count.

review.x: Factor \(8ab+12ac\) fully. Type the greatest common factor pulled out front, written like \(5x\) (number first, letters alphabetical).
hints: Take the GCD of \(8\) and \(12\), then ask which letters are in BOTH terms.
review.sol: The GCD of \(8\) and \(12\) is \(4\), and \(a\) is the only letter in both terms, so the GCF is \(\boxed{4a}\). The \(b\) and \(c\) each appear once, so neither comes out front.

review.x: Factor \(6cdh+15cdk\) fully. Type the greatest common factor, written like \(2xy\) (number first, letters alphabetical).
hints: Take the GCD of \(6\) and \(9\) first.
Which letters appear in BOTH terms? The \(r\) and \(s\) do not.
review.sol: The GCD of \(6\) and \(15\) is \(3\), and both \(c\) and \(d\) sit in every term, so the GCF is \(\boxed{3cd}\). The \(h\) and \(k\) each appear in only one term, so they stay inside.

review.x: Evaluate \(5st-2s+t\) at \(s=2,\ t=3\). Type the value.
hints: \(5st\) needs both letters, \(5\cdot s\cdot t\); handle \(-2s\) and \(+t\) after.
review.sol: \(5\cdot2\cdot3=30\), \(-2\cdot2=-4\), and \(+3\), so \(30-4+3=\boxed{29}\). The \(5st\) term needs both values, and reading it as \(5s\) drops the \(t\).
